newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa plans 10 bln rand assault on water needs.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa plans 10 bln rand assault on water needs.

text.p: South Africa has published for comment a draft Water Services Act that sets a timetable for the provision of sanitation to almost half the population and water to more than 12 million people who do not have it.

Mike Muller, deputy director general in the department of water affairs and forestry, said the government expected to commit a billion rand ($0.2 billion) a year over the next decade to the water programme for rural areas alone.

"This bill, for the first time, sets in place a national framework for the supply and provision of water services. Its main objective is to provide for the right of access of all South Africans to basic water and sanitation," he told members of a pariamentary committee.
Muller told Reuters the department estimated that 12 million of South Africa's 44 million people did not have safe water and about 21 million people had no safe sanitation.
He said the 10 billion rand ($2.2 billion) programme would largely address the backlog in the provision of water, but not of sanitation.
The bill proposed a national network of water supply and service authorities and a framework of norms and standards covering quality, reach and pricing of water supplies.
It entrenched the obligation to pay for water and proposes fines and prison sentences of up to two years for wastage.
The bill, which would overtake 19 existing acts going back to 1919, establishes the right to basic water and sanitation and requires authorities to "take reasonable measures to realise this right."

It requires every water services authority to draw up a development plan within a year of the adoption of the act, which is likely this year, setting out its programme for the extension of water services.
Authorities are required to identify all those who will not be brought into the supply network within five years, to explain why and to set out plans to include them.
Though the bill targets domestic water services, it gives local water authorities a veto over industrial water and sanitation plans.
Existing industrial rights to water and to dispose of waste will continue for five years, whereafter industrial users will have to meet water authority standards within an agreed time.
"To support municipalities and to help build capacity, we allow the water services authorities to regulate industrial water supply and sanitation," said legal adviser Robyn Steyn.
